opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think robotics is one of those areas where people have been a little bit confused about what the bottleneck actually is. For a long time the assumption was that the hard part is the hardware: the actuators, the sensors, the cost of the physical components. And those things matter, but I think a lot of what's held robotics back is really an intelligence problem. It's the ability to handle the long tail of situations in the physical world, to generalize, to recover when something goes wrong. That's exactly the kind of thing these models are getting better at.

So when you have models that can both design and control robots, I think a couple of things happen. On the control side, you get to the point where a model can look at a novel environment, a kitchen it's never seen, a factory floor that's been rearranged, and just figure it out the way a person would. That's the piece that's been missing. The robots we have today are often very capable in a narrow, carefully engineered setting and then fall apart outside of it.

On the design side, I think it's actually underrated. If you have something like a country of geniuses in a data center, some of those geniuses are going to be very good mechanical engineers, materials scientists, control theorists. They can iterate on designs in simulation much faster than human teams can, and then test the most promising ones in the real world. So you could see the design cycle compress dramatically.

Now, I want to be careful here, because the physical world has its own speed limits. You have to actually build things. You have to manufacture them, you have supply chains, you have safety testing, you have regulation. Intelligence doesn't make those constraints disappear. So I don't think it's going to be like flipping a switch where one day the models are smart and the next day there are billions of robots everywhere. I think it's more that the intelligence bottleneck gets removed, and then you're bottlenecked on the physical stuff, which moves more slowly but still faster than people expect once there's real economic pull.

And then, of course, there are the implications. Once AI can act in the physical world at scale, a lot of the questions we think about around safety, around concentration of power, around economic disruption, become much more concrete. A model that can only write text is one thing. A model that can operate machinery, build things, and potentially build more robots is a different level of capability. So I think it's very important that we get the alignment and the controllability right before that transition really takes off, not after.

r001.rationale: The response says models could iterate on designs much faster than human teams, but does not clearly predict that they will design better robots than humans.

r002.rationale: It says robotics will not transform overnight, citing manufacturing, supply chains, safety testing, and regulation as constraints that slow deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that robotics is going to lag a bit behind what's happening in the purely cognitive domain, but when it catches up, it's going to catch up fast, and the reason it catches up fast is exactly the thing you're pointing at.

Let me separate two things. One is the control problem, actually getting a robot to pick up a cup or walk across uneven ground. The other is the design problem, deciding what the robot should look like, what actuators it should have, what the sensors are, how it's manufactured. Historically those have been done by different groups of people on very different timescales. Control you can iterate on in simulation in days. Hardware design has cycles of months or years, and it's bottlenecked on a relatively small number of very skilled mechanical and electrical engineers.

What I expect is that the models eat the control problem first, and I think we're already seeing that. The same thing that happened with language, where you stop hand-engineering and you let a general model learn from enormous amounts of data, is happening with manipulation and locomotion. The data is harder to get, that's the real constraint, but it's a constraint that gets relaxed as you have more robots in the world generating data, and as simulation gets good enough that sim-to-real stops being a research problem.

The more interesting shift is on the design side. Right now a robot is designed by humans who have intuitions about what's buildable, and then a controller is fitted to it afterward. Once you have a model that's genuinely good at both, you can co-design. You can say, here's the task distribution, here are the manufacturing constraints, here's the cost target, and the model proposes a body and a brain together and evaluates thousands of variants. Humans do a little bit of this today but it's extremely laborious. A model that's doing the work of, you know, a hundred very good engineers running in parallel can explore that space in a way nobody's ever explored it. I think you'd end up with designs that look a bit strange to us, because they're not constrained by our priors about what a robot is supposed to look like.

And then there's a feedback loop, which is the thing I actually find myself thinking about most. If the models can design robots, and robots can build and maintain the factories and the labs, then the physical world starts to move at something closer to the speed of the digital world. I've written about this idea of a country of geniuses in a datacenter. The question people reasonably ask is, okay, but geniuses who can't touch anything, how much can they really do? Robotics is the answer to that question. It's how the intelligence gets hands.

Now, I want to be careful. There are hard physical limits here that don't go away no matter how smart the models are. You still have to mine the materials, you still have to ship things, you still have to run experiments in the real world that take as long as they take. Biology doesn't speed up because you have a better experiment designer. So I don't expect some overnight transformation. What I expect is that over a period of, let's say, five to fifteen years, the cost of physical labor and physical manufacturing starts to fall on a curve that looks more like the cost of compute has fallen than like the cost of, you know, building a house has fallen. And that's an enormous change, because most of the economy is still atoms, not bits.

The last thing I'd say is that this is one of the areas where I think about the safety and the geopolitical side a lot. A world where AI can design and control robots at scale is a world where the physical capacity of whoever controls those systems increases very quickly. That's true for good things, it's true for manufacturing, it's true for defense. So I don't think you can look at this purely as a technology story. It raises the stakes on all the questions we already have about who builds these systems and under what constraints.

r001.rationale: The response says models could co-design robot bodies and controllers, evaluate thousands of variants, and explore the design space beyond what human teams have managed, predicting stronger design capability than humans can achieve alone.

r002.rationale: It says robotics will lag behind cognitive AI, warns against expecting an overnight transformation, and describes change unfolding over five to fifteen years.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much of robotics is a problem of intelligence, and how much is a problem of the physical hardware and the process of deploying it. If the models can design robots, write the control software, and learn new tasks reliably, then you’ve removed a very large part of the bottleneck.

But you still have to build the robots. You have to manufacture motors and batteries, you have to test them, and you have to make sure they can operate safely in a messy environment. Those things take time in a way that copying a piece of software doesn’t.

So I would expect a lag, but potentially a very rapid acceleration after that lag. And there’s a feedback loop: better AI helps you design better robots, and those robots can help you manufacture things and run experiments, which gives the AI more ability to affect the physical world.

The uncertainty is whether that initial lag is relatively short or whether the engineering and manufacturing constraints remain binding for a long time. I wouldn’t assume that solving the intelligence part means you get billions of useful robots the next day. But I also wouldn’t extrapolate from the slow progress we’ve seen when so much of the work has had to be done by humans, one task at a time.

r001.rationale: It says AI can design robots and improve them, but does not claim models will design robots better than humans.

r002.rationale: It predicts a lag due to manufacturing, testing, and deployment constraints, and says billions of useful robots will not appear the next day.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different things here. One is controlling a robot that already exists: can the model understand what’s happening around it, make a plan, and reliably execute that plan? The other is designing better hardware. Progress on the first doesn’t automatically solve the second.

My guess is that, initially, we’ll see existing robots become much more useful. You won’t need to write a separate program for every task. You’ll be able to explain what you want, and the robot will adapt to circumstances it hasn’t encountered before. But reliability is a very demanding constraint. A system that succeeds 95 percent of the time can be impressive in a demonstration and still be pretty frustrating in your house or a factory.

Then, if models become good enough at engineering, they could help improve the robots themselves—designing components, interpreting experimental results, figuring out why something failed. That could accelerate progress substantially. But you still have to build things and test them in the physical world. Manufacturing takes time.

So I’d expect a potentially very rapid improvement in the intelligence available to robots, followed by a more uneven process of turning that intelligence into useful physical capabilities. I’m uncertain about how long that second part takes.

r001.rationale: The response says models could help improve robot hardware, but it does not predict they will design robots better than humans can.

r002.rationale: It says physical capabilities will improve unevenly because robots must be built and tested and manufacturing takes time, rather than transforming instantly.
